Tony Blair. The architect of New Labour and the longest-serving Labour Prime Minister in British history, transforming the party through modernization and centralism.

Blair's tenure from 1997 to 2007 oversaw constitutional devolution, the Northern Ireland peace process, and Britain's controversial involvement in the Iraq War. He won three consecutive landslide elections in 1997, 2001, and 2005, giving Labour unprecedented consecutive terms in power and reshaping the party as a centrist, market-friendly force. This represented a fundamental transformation of Labour from its socialist tradition into a modern center-left coalition.

In 1997, Blair implemented devolution to Scotland and Wales, granting them their own parliaments for the first time in centuries and rebalancing the union's internal power structure. He played a central role in the Northern Ireland peace process, culminating in the Good Friday Agreement of 1998, which established power-sharing and ended decades of conflict and violence.

Blair expanded the welfare state through targeted tax credits and education investment, combining market liberalism with targeted welfare spending in a synthesis he called Third Way politics. However, he led Britain into the 2003 Iraq War alongside the United States, claiming Saddam Hussein possessed weapons of mass destruction. The war's justification was later discredited, damaging Blair's credibility. He resigned in 2007 before the Iraq War's full consequences and the financial crash became apparent, departing as one of Britain's most celebrated and most controversial postwar leaders.
